title: Algorithms & Problem-Solving in C
relevance: SDE interviews and OAs expect candidates to analyze complexity, choose search/sort approaches on raw arrays, and avoid C-specific pitfalls like overflow-safe mid and safe qsort comparators.

phases.goal: Establish asymptotic complexity vocabulary and when linear vs binary search apply.

must_hit.point: Big-O is the asymptotic upper bound (worst-case): f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for some constant c as n → ∞; Big-Omega is the lower bound (best-case); Big-Theta is the tight bound from both sides.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate distinguishes O / Ω / Θ and states that largest scaling term dominates after dropping constants and smaller terms.

must_hit.point: We evaluate algorithms by counting fundamental operations relative to input size n for both time (CPU work) and space (extra memory), not by stopwatch timing on a specific machine.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions mathematical scaling as n grows large and rejects wall-clock timing because of CPU, load, and compiler effects.

must_hit.point: Linear search inspects every element sequentially: O(n) time and O(1) space, and is the only viable option for completely unsorted, unstructured data.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States sequential scan costs and that unsorted data forces linear search.

must_hit.point: Binary search on an already sorted array checks the middle element and halves the search space each step, yielding O(log n) time.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes mid check, left/right half restriction, and O(log n) cost on sorted input.

probes: How do Big-O, Big-Omega, and Big-Theta differ, and why do we drop constants and lower-order terms?
When would you use linear search versus binary search on an array?

hints.1: Think about upper vs lower vs tight growth rates as n gets huge.
hints.2: Relate each bound to worst/best/tight case, then contrast sequential scan vs halving a sorted array.
hints.3: O is upper/worst, Ω lower/best, Θ tight; linear is O(n)/O(1) for unsorted data; binary is O(log n) only if sorted.

phases.goal: Check how binary search, divide-and-conquer sorts, stdlib search/sort, and common array patterns actually work in C.

must_hit.point: Overflow-safe middle index is mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2; writing mid = (lo + hi) / 2 can overflow a signed int when lo and hi are large (undefined behavior).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Gives the safe formula and names signed integer overflow as the bug with (lo + hi) / 2.

must_hit.point: Merge sort recursively halves until size 1 then merges sorted halves: guarantees O(n log n) time, needs O(n) auxiliary space, and is stable (identical elements keep relative order).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions recursive halving, merge step, O(n log n) time, O(n) aux space, and stability.

must_hit.point: Quicksort picks a pivot and partitions so smaller elements are left and larger right; typically in-place with O(log n) recursion-stack space and very fast in practice.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes pivot/partition and in-place practice with O(log n) stack space.

must_hit.point: qsort and bsearch in <stdlib.h> take opaque void * plus element size and a comparator that returns negative/zero/positive for less/equal/greater.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names void *, size argument, and the three-way comparator contract.

must_hit.point: Common array patterns: two-pointer (indices at 0 and n - 1 moving inward), sliding-window (start/end subarray expanding/shrinking), and in-place partitioning by swapping without O(n) extra space.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Can name at least two patterns and what the indices do.

probes: Why is mid = (lo + hi) / 2 unsafe in C binary search, and what do you write instead?
How does merge sort achieve O(n log n), and what space/stability properties does it have?

hints.1: Focus on how indices and recursion actually update, not just Big-O labels.
hints.2: For binary search, talk about int overflow; for merge sort, recursive halves plus temp buffer.
hints.3: Safe mid is lo + (hi - lo) / 2; merge sort is O(n log n) time, O(n) aux, stable; quicksort partitions around a pivot.

phases.goal: Judge when quadratic vs n log n sorts, merge vs quicksort, and recursion vs iteration are the right call.

must_hit.point: Bubble, insertion, and selection sort are O(n²) and generally too slow for large data, but insertion sort is highly efficient for very small or nearly sorted arrays.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names the quadratic family and carves out insertion sort for small/nearly sorted inputs.

must_hit.point: Merge sort guarantees O(n log n) but pays O(n) auxiliary space; quicksort is typically in-place and fast in practice but can degrade depending on pivots.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts guaranteed merge cost/space with quicksort’s practical speed and pivot sensitivity.

must_hit.point: Recursion expresses divide-and-conquer elegantly (e.g. merge sort’s T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n)) but each call uses stack space and deep recursion can stack-overflow; iterative solutions are safer for massive inputs but often harder to read.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States the simplicity-vs-stack-depth tradeoff and mentions stack overflow risk.

must_hit.point: Asymptotic ranking can fail for very small n: an O(n²) algorithm may beat an O(n log n) one on tiny arrays due to lower constant overhead.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Notes that Big-O compares growth for large n and constants can dominate on tiny inputs.

probes: When would you prefer insertion sort over merge sort or quicksort?
What do you gain and lose by implementing divide-and-conquer recursively versus iteratively?

hints.1: Compare guaranteed bounds, extra memory, and input shape (small vs large, nearly sorted).
hints.2: Put merge’s aux buffer and stability against quicksort’s in-place speed; put stack depth against readability.
hints.3: Insertion for small/nearly sorted; merge guarantees O(n log n) with O(n) space; recursion risks stack overflow on deep calls.

phases.goal: Apply interview process, C library pitfalls, bit tricks, and known algorithm failure modes.

must_hit.point: Interview flow: clarify bounds/types/edge cases (e.g. empty arrays); state a brute-force baseline; optimize (hash map, sorting first); manually trace size 0, 1, and 2 before finishing.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Walks clarify → brute force → optimize → edge-trace with tiny arrays.

must_hit.point: Quicksort worst-case time is O(n²) when the pivot is consistently the smallest or largest element each step (e.g. first element on an already sorted array); mitigate with a random pivot or median-of-three.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States O(n²), bad pivot pattern, and random/median-of-three mitigation.

must_hit.point: Integer qsort comparators must not return *(int*)a - *(int*)b: large positive minus large negative can overflow and flip the sign; use explicit if/else comparisons.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Rejects subtraction comparator and describes if/else returning negative/zero/positive.

must_hit.point: Bit tricks: (x & (x - 1)) == 0 checks power of two for x > 0; repeated x &= (x - 1) clears set bits for popcount; XOR of pairs leaves the unique element when every other value appears twice.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Can explain at least one of power-of-two, popcount-via-clear-lowest-set-bit, or XOR unique.

probes: What is quicksort’s worst-case complexity, when does it happen, and how do you mitigate it?
Why is returning a - b unsafe in an int comparator for qsort, and what should you do instead?

hints.1: Think about adversarial pivots and overflow in arithmetic on int values.
hints.2: Worst case is consistently bad pivots; comparator bug is subtraction overflow, not just wrong logic.
hints.3: Worst case O(n²) on always extreme pivots—use random or median-of-three; compare ints with if/else, not subtraction.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: Reject timing with a stopwatch: elapsed time depends on CPU, system load, and compiler optimizations. Prefer counting how operations and memory scale with n via Big-O / Ω / Θ.
Linear search is O(n) time / O(1) space and works on unsorted data. Binary search is O(log n) but requires a sorted array and careful mid/boundary handling.

tradeoffs.topic: Quadratic sorts vs O(n log n) sorts
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Bubble/insertion/selection are O(n²) and usually too slow for large datasets; insertion sort still shines on very small or nearly sorted arrays. Merge sort and quicksort target O(n log n) via divide-and-conquer.
Merge sort guarantees O(n log n), uses O(n) auxiliary space, and is stable. Quicksort is typically in-place (O(log n) stack), very fast in practice, but pivot choice can degrade performance.
Recursion matches the recurrence cleanly but each call consumes stack space and deep recursion can stack-overflow. Iteration is safer for massive inputs but often harder to read.

gotchas.trap: Assuming two nested loops are always O(n²).
gotchas.correction: If the outer loop runs n times but the inner loop halves its workload each step, total cost may be O(n log n). Always count exact iterations.

gotchas.trap: Computing mid as (lo + hi) / 2 in binary search.
gotchas.correction: lo + hi can overflow a signed int (undefined behavior). Use mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2.

gotchas.trap: Running binary search on data that is not strictly sorted, or needing the first of duplicate keys without adjusting boundaries.
gotchas.correction: Binary search requires sorted order; duplicates need explicit boundary logic (e.g. for first occurrence), not the plain mid equality check alone.

gotchas.trap: Writing an int qsort comparator as *(int*)a - *(int*)b.
gotchas.correction: Subtraction can overflow and flip the comparison sign. Compare with explicit if/else and return negative, zero, or positive.

gotchas.trap: Relying on recursion for huge divide-and-conquer inputs.
gotchas.correction: Deep recursion can exceed OS stack limits and crash. Prefer iterative approaches when inputs are massive.

gotchas.trap: Expecting in-memory sorts to handle data that does not fit in main memory.
gotchas.correction: Standard array sorts break there; use specialized external sorting techniques instead.
